topicA.name: B2B SEO in the Age of AI Search

resources.headline: AI Mode Queries Are 3X Longer – Why Your Page Should Lead With The Answer via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: SEO practitioners who rely on long-form narrative arcs to keep users on a page are losing ground to automated search synthesis. Google AI Overviews compress multi-source information into immediate factual summaries, requiring content architects to prioritize immediate data retrieval over traditional brand storytelling. If your pages bury the primary answer, you make it harder for the systems that assemble AI Mode responses to pull a usable passage. How can you verify this for yourself? Start by reading “How AI Mode Is Changing The Way People Search In The U.S.,” which was written by Shivani Mohan, Google’s vice president, Data Science and UXR, and published on the Google blog on May 19, 2026. The Query Itself Has Changed Shape AI Mode has passed 1 billion monthly active users globally, and queries have more than doubled every quarter since launch. But the volume number is the least interesting part of this story. What’s more interesting is that people aren’t just searching more frequently; they’re asking questions differently. The average AI Mode query in the U.S. is triple the length of a traditional search query, and more than one in six AI Mode searches now include something other than text, whether that’s an image, voice, or a live back-and-forth conversation. Image-based queries are growing more than 40% month over month. Follow-up questions are climbing at the same rate. People start a search, then keep going, refining and narrowing in a way that looks nothing like the one-shot keyword query that SEO strategy has been built around for two decades. Google’s own list of the most common first words in AI Mode queries confirms it. “What,” “how,” “I,” “is,” and “can” now lead the pack, not short-head nouns. People are asking questions the way they’d ask another person, not typing fragments the way they’d type into a search box. 5 Verbs Replaced The Keyword Mohan’s report groups the new behavior into five modes: Explore, Decide, Learn, Create, and Do. Each one maps to a distinct kind of content need, and each is growing at a different rate. Explore queries, the open-ended, brainstorming kind, are growing 30% faster than AI Mode traffic overall. Decide queries built around comparison words like “which of” and “which one” are growing 40% faster. Learn queries help people understand new concepts and explore professional development opportunities. Do queries tied to planning, from workout routines to travel itineraries to household budgets, are growing 80% faster than AI Mode queries overall over the past six months. Image creation queries in AI Mode have more than tripled since the start of the year. None of these maps cleanly onto a keyword. They map onto a task. That’s the shift, and it’s the one that clearly indicates we’re not on a relatively shorter, straightforward journey to plot a course around ranking-factor changes. We’re on a significantly longer, more complicated odyssey to navigate user-behavior transformation. What This Means For Your Content Strategy If you’re still building content briefs around a head term and related keywords, this data says that model is aging out in real time, not in some hypothetical AI-search future. So, how should you change your content strategy this quarter? Follow the lead of journalists, who traditionally wrote stories chronologically – until a new technology, the telegraph, changed their writing style in the 19th century. The transition to a lead-first structure became an industry standard between 1880 and 1890 due to simple economics and mechanical limits. The Associated Press paid telegraph operators by the word, making poetic preambles an unnecessary tax on profits. In newspaper back shops, editors assembling heavy metal type needed a reliable way to cut stories from the bottom up to fit physical page constraints without removing critical facts. Today, generative search engines operate under similar computational and mathematical constraints. I learned this lesson the hard way, decades before Google rolled out AI Overview. In 1986, as the newly minted director of corporate communications at Lotus, I proudly dropped a thick binder of press clippings on CEO Jim Manzi’s desk. He glanced at it and told me that until I could “measure the impact of PR in cold, hard cash,” he didn’t want to see my so-called reports. That line sent me down a 40-year rabbit hole into measurement, and it’s the same demand generative search is now making of every writer on the web: Stop burying the value, prove it immediately, or get skipped. In my judgment, trying to protect a vague brand voice by hiding core facts inside fluffy introductions is a fast track to search irrelevance. You do not need to turn your writing into sterile robot prose, but you must align your site architecture with how algorithmic synthesis processes data. 5 Practical Steps For AI-Driven Search Optimization Here are five concrete steps you can apply to your content strategy today to improve visibility in AI search summaries. 1. Lead With Entity-Dense Opening Sentences Place your primary definition, key metric, or main conclusion directly in the first sentence of every core section. Anchor your sentences with specific brand names, clear geographic markers, exact dates, and verified numerical values. Avoiding vague generalizations makes your prose mathematically readable for search engines and reduces the risk of AI hallucination. 2. Implement Scannable Hybrid Layouts Organize body copy into short paragraphs that average two or three sentences. Follow major section headers with concise summaries, ordered lists, or structured tables. This approach allows search crawlers to extract clean segments for generated overviews while giving human readers a frictionless scanning experience. 3. Write For The Follow-Up, Not Just The First Click If more than 40% month-over-month growth is happening in multi-turn conversations, your content needs to answer the second and third question a reader would ask after th
keyNotes: Surprisingly, when people use AI search, their questions are three times longer than traditional searches, and they ask full questions like "What" or "How" instead of just a few words. This means they are talking to the search engine more like a person.

People are increasingly using AI search to accomplish specific tasks, such as planning a trip or comparing products, rather than just looking for a single piece of information. For instance, searches related to planning or 'doing' things are growing 80% faster.

To make sure your website content is found by AI, you need to put the main answer or most important facts right at the very beginning. This is similar to how journalists changed their writing style for the telegraph, putting critical information first so it wouldn't get cut.

To help AI understand your content, start your sentences with clear facts, specific names, dates, and numbers. Also, organize your information into short paragraphs and lists, making it easy for AI to quickly pull out key details.
resources.question: The article suggests that just like journalists changed their writing for the telegraph by putting the most important information first, we now need to 'lead with the answer' for AI search. In your own work, where do you currently 'bury the lead' or save the most important information for later, and how might immediately sharing that key insight change how people interact with what you present?

resources.headline: The House Doesn’t Publish Its Tells via @sejournal, @pedrodias
resources.fullText: AI companies are buying pallets of old printed books. Physical books, paper and glue, the format the entire industry was supposed to have made quaint. ISBNdb, a broker that sources bulk print acquisitions for AI labs, pitches it with a straight face: “The world’s best AI training data is sitting on a shelf.” And the pitch works, because books have one property no amount of prompt engineering can fake. They were printed before the slop existed. So the companies that built the slop machines are paying real money to avoid eating the output of the slop machines. Meanwhile, an entire vendor category is charging you monthly to feed those same companies as much machine output as you can generate. Someone in this supply chain has misread the room. The Measurement Went First Old search was deterministic enough to build an industry on. A ranking was a position, a position produced impressions and clicks, and clicks carried tracking parameters into analytics that told you what converted. You could argue about attribution windows for hours, and God knows we did, but the pipeline held still long enough to be measured. AI answers hold still for no one. Ask the same question twice, and the brands can change. There is structure under the noise, a distribution whose stability depends on the corpus behind it and the quality of the prompts probing it, but here’s the thing about the probing: It’s synthetic. Your tracker fires sterile prompts at an API and gets back answers stripped of the context and personalization that shape what actual humans see. Even a perfectly stable reading is likely a perfectly stable reading of the wrong thing. A more honest industry might have stopped here. Ours built dashboards. Position tracking for a system with no positions, share of voice for answers nobody’s session will ever reproduce, all reported with the decimal-point confidence of a rank report from 2014. And on the production side, the same vendors sell the thing this piece is actually about: AI-generated content, at scale, optimized for retrieval by systems whose owners are building the tools to identify it. The Infrastructure Is Already At Internet Scale On 19 May (at I/O 2026), Google announced that SynthID, its invisible watermarking system, had marked more than 100 billion AI-generated images and videos plus roughly 60,000 years of audio, with verification rolling into Search immediately and Chrome in the weeks after. Same day, OpenAI committed to embedding SynthID in every image generated through ChatGPT, Codex and the API. Kakao and ElevenLabs are on the partner list; NVIDIA joined earlier through its Cosmos models. This is what provenance looks like when it stops being a research demo and starts being plumbing. I can hear the objection from here: that’s images and audio, and the content farms sell text. Correct. OpenAI’s commitment covers images only, and Google’s published text watermarking comes with documented weaknesses. DeepMind says detection confidence drops sharply when text is thoroughly rewritten or translated, and the method struggles on short factual outputs. Plenty of people have read exactly that far and concluded AI text at scale is safe. Comforting … also lazy. It’s also, as of August, out of date. Anthropic has signed the EU AI Act’s Code of Practice on transparency and published its plan: Claude models launched from August 2, 2026 onwards are to embed watermarks in generated text at the model level, applied worldwide, across the API, the consumer apps and the cloud platforms. The legal trigger is European, but the watermark ships inside the model, so a Brussels mandate becomes the global default. Anthropic says it will help third parties detect the watermarking, with the mechanism described in “forthcoming technical documentation,” a phrase I encourage you to savor. Their own page notes the mark doesn’t certify authorship either: text merely processed by Claude, proofread, translated, tidied up, can carry it. And the published limitations are the familiar ones: heavy editing, translation, very short passages, which are, as ever, the limitations of what’s been chosen for publication. The open-source SynthID text repository carries a note from DeepMind itself: the code is a reference implementation for the research paper, “not intended for production use,” with a hashing function offering no cryptographic security guarantees. Read that again, slowly. The version you can inspect is, by Google’s own description, not the version that runs. Everyone confidently citing the published limitations is citing the limitations of a demo. I spent nearly six years inside Google’s search quality and webspam teams, so let me save you some suspense about how this works. Google has never published how spam detection operated. Ever. Publishing the mechanism is handing over the evasion manual, and every serious detection system in the history of search has been built on that silence. The idea that the same company would now document its AI text detection honestly, for the convenience of the people it’s designed to catch, is genuinely sweet. If a text watermarking or detection method that survives paraphrasing exists or arrives, the first you will hear of it or how it works is never. The evasion side turned up right on schedule, of course. Within days of Anthropic’s announcement, a watermark remover appeared on GitHub, covering Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI, and its README is more honest than most of the GEO industry. For statistical text watermarks, its method is a heavy rewrite through another model, labelled best-effort, and it concedes that until vendors ship public detectors, “no tool can honestly certify” the mark is gone. It even recommends laundering Claude text through a different model, in case the rinse re-stamps the washing. That’s the mouse’s side of the game in full: scrubbing invisible characters and hoping that was the watermark, paraphrasing against a detector nobody can query, and shipping with a dis
keyNotes: Surprisingly, AI companies are buying physical books to train their systems because these books contain original human-created content, which is seen as higher quality than content already generated by AI. This highlights a challenge in finding pure, untainted data for AI.

The traditional ways of measuring how well online content performs, like tracking its position in search results, don't work for AI-generated answers. This is because AI's responses can change every time you ask, making consistent measurement impossible.

Even though AI answers are unstable, many companies are still selling tools that claim to measure things like "share of voice" (how often your brand is mentioned) for AI content. The article points out that these tools might be giving a false sense of accuracy because the data they're tracking is constantly changing.

Major tech companies like Google and Anthropic are trying to embed invisible "watermarks" into AI-generated content (like images, audio, and text) to help identify it. For instance, Google's system, called SynthID, has already marked over 100 billion AI-created images and videos.

Despite these efforts, watermarking for AI-generated text has known weaknesses, as detection can fail if the text is heavily rewritten or translated. In fact, tools designed to remove these watermarks have already started to appear, showing the ongoing challenge of identifying AI content.
resources.question: The article points out that even with efforts to watermark AI-generated text, detection can be difficult if the content is heavily rewritten, and tools to remove watermarks already exist. In your own work, how do you currently assess the authenticity and trustworthiness of information or content, especially when it might have been subtly altered or 'laundered' without your knowledge?

keyNotes: The way people search online is dramatically changing: Instead of just typing keywords, people are now having conversations with AI tools like Perplexity and ChatGPT. These tools prioritize a company's overall reputation (brand authority) over simple keyword matching, meaning businesses need a new strategy to be found.

Your company's older information could be a hidden risk with AI: Artificial intelligence is constantly analyzing all your past publications (old content), which means businesses need to understand what AI is learning about their brand from everything they've ever shared.

It's now essential to create content that both people and AI can trust: The goal is to build information that is reliable and credible for both human readers and the artificial intelligence systems that process and present information.

Many specific, actionable strategies exist to make your content better: The article points to various practical approaches, such as 5 steps to simplify future content updates, 8 questions to craft compelling headlines, or 19 low-cost marketing tactics that deliver results.

How you arrange your content matters more than ever: Instead of just rigid categories (hierarchy), businesses should focus on organizing their information based on its overall meaning and relevance (context) to help audiences find and understand it better.
resources.question: Given that AI search now rewards a company's overall reputation (brand authority) rather than just specific keywords, how might you need to rethink the way your organization presents itself and its information to build that trust, even if you're not directly in marketing?

keyNotes: Surprisingly, understanding what your sales team (the people who talk directly to customers) wishes you knew is crucial for actually landing sales, not just talking to other marketers.
There are specific methods or "systems" that claim to help you quickly generate interest in your product or service, with one even suggesting it can be done in just 39 days.
Making your sales team happy and effective often comes down to creating content (like articles or videos) that directly matches what potential customers are looking for.
Despite all the buzz, new research suggests that artificial intelligence (AI) isn't a magical fix for creating customer interest; it's not a "knight in shining armor."
It's important to help even company leaders understand the value of content marketing (creating useful information for customers) if they seem "clueless" about its impact.

keyNotes: Building a strong group of followers (an "audience") for your business isn't just about getting their attention; it's about turning them into dedicated, loyal communities, like turning base metals into gold ("alchemy").
To earn the trust of other businesses (B2B), you need to show them what you can actually do, which is called "proof of work," and actively gain their attention in various ways, not just expect it.
Even with many new ways to reach people, having your own website and creating your own content ("owned content") remains a powerful way to connect directly with your audience.
To truly understand what your audience wants, looking at data (like website visits) isn't enough; having actual conversations can reveal insights that numbers alone cannot.
The places where your audience spends their time online are constantly shifting, so you must regularly update how and where you share your content to keep reaching them effectively.
